newsitem.title: GERMANY: Dlr boosts profit at German drugs, chemical firms.
newsitem.headline: Dlr boosts profit at German drugs, chemical firms.

text.p: The dollar's strength against the mark boosted first-quarter 1997 earnings at German drugs group Schering AG and chemicals and pharmaceuticals group Bayer AG, both released on Wednesday.

But analysts said that full-year outlooks for the two firms were widely different. The outlook was better for Schering because of its focus on drugs while Bayer was vulnerable to cyclical factors because of its chemicals business.

A London-based pharmaceuticals analyst, who did not wish to be named, said: "Schering is doing well because it is a very focused pharmaceutical company. You're also seeing the positive impact of the dollar."

Even taking Bayer's pharmaceutical business on its own, its performance was viewed as disappointing, with much of the growth related to the dollar's strength against the mark rather than any fundamental improvement in Bayer's drugs business.

"Looking at Bayer's sales growth in the pharmaceutical sector, it was up nine percent. But if you strip out currency benefits it looks weaker," said Penny Tattersall, chemicals analyst at Credit Suisse First Boston in London.

The differing fortunes of the two groups were reflected in their share performance. Schering ended bourse trade on the DAX index up five marks ($2.89) at 166 marks, while Bayer ended the day down eight pfennigs at 68.90.

Schering said its profits for the first quarter of 1997 had risen between 10 and 15 percent from a year earlier and said that the current dollar/mark exchange rate would boost profits for the year as whole by around 10 to 15 percent.

The outlook at Bayer was less positive. It took the market by surprise when it said it expected profits in 1997 to be at least in line with 1996's 2.7 billion marks and that it expected 1997 group sales of over 50 billion marks.

This forecast was more downbeat than last month, when the group said it had a realistic chance of topping 1996 profits this year, and profits and sales for this year were at the lower end of analysts' expectations.

"The Bayer figures were below expectations. I think a lot of people had a look at the first quarter figures in the light of the forecast for a strong start to the year, which doesn't seem to have happened," said Tattersall.

Bayer's first-quarter 1997 pre-tax profits rose five percent to 1.218 billion marks on turnover of 13.172 billion marks, up from 12.176 billion, Bayer said, while sales in 1996 totalled 48.6 billion marks.
Schering's board chairman Giuseppe Vita told the firm's annual meeting that the first three months of this year had developed very favourably due to the dollar/mark level.
The mark has weakened substantially against the dollar in recent months and was trading at 1.7275 in mid-morning trade on Wednesday.
German pharmaceuticals groups are big exporters and the weakness of the mark helped boost the competitiveness of their products abroad.

"Bayer has seen a big rise in launch costs, in research and development costs and then there is the chemicals sector, which is not experiencing significant growth in Europe - these all contributed to the first-quarter figures," said Tattersall.

Elsewhere in the sector, sales at drugs wholesaler Andreae-Noris Zahn AG (Anzag) in the first half of the 1996/97 financial year fell to 2.096 billion marks from 2.139 billion, although first-half income from ordinary activities was up 14.2 percent, at 39.0 million marks.
Revenues in the first half of the financial year, which runs from September 1996 to August 1997, were hit by falling demand in the pharmaceuticals market, Anzag said.
